feature_request: The CRM should alert us when our relationship with a country goes cold.

proposed_scope_in.item: Define 'cold' as a deterministic rule over existing Engagement records: a country is cold when its most recent logged Engagement (any Contact, any Project or Mission, any channel) is older than a single global threshold of 90 days. No new fields for Regional Coordinators to fill in.

A nightly scheduled job evaluates every active Country against the S1 rule and writes a derived, system-filled status (last_engagement_date, is_cold, cold_since) on the existing Country entity. No new tables and no manual input.

Suppress or pause the cold flag for a Country while it has at least one active Mission or a Mission/Project with a scheduled future Engagement, since the relationship is evidently being worked. The rule reads existing Mission/Project data only.

When a Country transitions from not-cold to cold, send one in-app notification and one email to the Regional Coordinator already assigned to that Country in the existing CRM. Fires once per transition, with no repeat reminders. The message contains the country name, the date of last engagement, and a link to the Country record.

Show a read-only 'Cold' badge and 'last engaged N days ago' on the existing Country record and in the existing Country list view, and make it filterable. The badge and alert content use the existing Country access permissions, so users who cannot view a Country cannot see its cold status or alerts.
The flag clears automatically the next nightly run after any new Engagement is logged for the Country. No acknowledge, snooze or dismiss workflow.

proposed_scope_out: Per-country, per-contact, or per-relationship-tier configurable thresholds
Relationship health scoring, sentiment analysis, or any ML/predictive model
Snooze, acknowledge, assign, or escalation workflows and alert queues
New dashboards, cold-country lists, or reports beyond the filter on the existing Country list view
Alerts for individual contacts going cold (e.g., a ministry contact leaving) as opposed to the country as a whole
Engagement quality weighting (e.g., a courtesy email versus a ministerial meeting)
Automatic ingestion of engagement from email, calendar, or other external systems
Adding new manual fields to be filled in by Regional Coordinators
Defining which countries are diplomatically sensitive or setting clearance rules: this is a policy and classification matter for humans, so v1 inherits existing access controls only
Backfilling or cleaning historical engagement data

assumptions.statement: 'Cold' means time elapsed since the last logged Engagement with the country, i.e. an absence of recorded contact, and not a qualitative judgement of relationship quality or sentiment.
assumptions.rationale: Elapsed time is computable from data the CRM already holds, so it needs no new entities and no coordinator input, and is explainable to any user in one sentence.

assumptions.statement: A single global 90-day threshold is an acceptable starting default for all ~100 countries, and the existing Engagement history is logged consistently enough for it to be meaningful.
assumptions.rationale: A single constant avoids a per-country settings screen that someone would have to maintain. The threshold is a single config value that can be tuned after observing real alert volumes, so it is cheap to correct after launch.

assumptions.statement: Every Country already has a Regional Coordinator (or equivalent owner) in the CRM, and the existing Country/Mission access model governs who may view a Country and its data.
assumptions.rationale: Reusing existing ownership and permissions means no routing tables or new RBAC. Alerts go to people who already have rights to the data, which bounds exposure.

assumptions.statement: Active Missions and scheduled future Engagements indicate a live relationship, so a country with them should not be flagged cold even if no Engagement was recently logged.
assumptions.rationale: This is a simple query over existing Mission/Project data that prevents the most obvious false alarms and alert fatigue, without any manual exemption flag.

assumptions.statement: The CRM already has in-app notification and email delivery capability that can be reused. If not, in-app notification and the badge alone are sufficient for v1.
assumptions.rationale: Reusing existing delivery channels avoids building new infrastructure. The badge and filter on the Country list work even without email.

success_criteria.criterion: The nightly job evaluates 100% of active Countries and completes within 15 minutes, with is_cold and last_engagement_date matching a manual spot-check of 20 sampled countries with zero discrepancies.

Each not-cold to cold transition produces exactly one notification to the assigned Regional Coordinator within 24 hours, with zero repeat alerts for the same cold episode, verified in the first 30 days post-launch.

Fewer than 10% of cold alerts in the first 60 days are reported by Regional Coordinators as false alarms (e.g., relationship was active but engagement was not logged), measured via a one-click 'not useful' link or a short feedback survey, used to decide whether to tune the threshold.
A user without access to a given Country sees no cold badge, filter result, or notification for it, verified with a permission test covering at least 3 role types.
After a new Engagement is logged for a cold Country, the cold flag clears by the next nightly run in 100% of test cases, with zero coordinator actions required.

challenges.challenge_text: The first nightly run after launch will flag every country whose engagement history is stale or was never logged consistently. Backfill is explicitly out of scope, and some countries are legitimately contacted only once or twice a year. Regional Coordinators across ~100 countries could receive dozens of 'cold' alerts on day one, most of them data-quality artifacts rather than real cooling. They learn to ignore the alert, and the real cold country is missed. A single 90-day threshold also fires constantly for low-tempo relationships and never for high-tempo ones. The 10% false-alarm criterion is measured only after 60 days of damage. There is no launch-time baselining or suppression of the initial transition storm.
challenges.evaluation_of_proposer: The proposer calls the threshold 'cheap to correct after launch' but does not address the day-one alert flood or the data-consistency assumption. Both are baked into A2 without evidence.

challenges.challenge_text: The alert goes once, to the single assigned Regional Coordinator, with no repeats. Coordinators turn over often across 100 countries. If the coordinator has left, is on leave, or the assignment is blank or stale, the one-time alert goes to a deactivated mailbox or nobody. Because the alert fires only once per transition, the country then stays cold in silence and nobody is ever told. The assumption that every Country has a valid, current owner is untested, and the design has no fallback recipient or 'no owner' detection.
challenges.evaluation_of_proposer: The proposer assumes ownership exists and is current, and offers no fallback. Turnover resilience is not addressed.

challenges.challenge_text: The derived last_engagement_date and is_cold are computed by a nightly job over ALL Engagement records for a country, then shown to anyone who can view the Country. Under least-privilege, a staff member may see a Country but not a restricted Mission, Contact, or Engagement. A user who sees 'last engaged 2 days ago' on a country where they know of no recent activity learns that a confidential engagement occurred. The same applies to a country that silently flips from cold to warm. S5 says Country permissions apply, but it does not say the derived value is computed per viewer's visible engagements or that restricted engagements are excluded or masked. The system-filled field on the Country entity bypasses record-level restrictions.
challenges.evaluation_of_proposer: The proposer treats 'use existing Country access permissions' as sufficient. That ignores that a derived aggregate over data the viewer cannot see leaks its existence and timing.

challenges.challenge_text: Suppression of the cold flag while a country has any 'active Mission' or any scheduled future Engagement creates false negatives. Missions are often left open long after real activity stops, and future engagements are often placeholders that get cancelled or never marked complete. A country with a zombie mission or a stale calendar entry is never flagged, even after a year of no real contact. This is exactly the relationship the feature should catch. When the mission is eventually closed, the country may flip to cold abruptly, with no engagement-age context. The proposal has no staleness bound on the suppressing mission or scheduled engagement, such as a cap on how long it can suppress.
challenges.evaluation_of_proposer: The proposer presents suppression as a simple fix for false alarms and does not address its own failure mode of masking genuinely cold countries.

challenges.challenge_text: The rule counts 'any Contact, any channel' as warming the relationship. An engagement logged with a ministry contact who has since left office, with a mission delegate unrelated to the host government, or a bulk or administrative entry such as a mass circular or an internal note logged as an Engagement, resets the 90-day clock. The country shows 'not cold' even though there is no live channel to anyone currently in post. Conversely, a country engaged only through a single departed minister's staff looks warm. 'Absence of recorded contact' is not the same as a working relationship when contact turnover is the main real-world risk. There is no filter on engagement type or on whether the contact is still active.
challenges.evaluation_of_proposer: The proposer defines cold purely as elapsed time since any logged engagement and does not consider that logged engagement may not reflect a live relationship.

challenges.challenge_text: S4 sends email containing the country name and 'gone cold' status. Email leaves the CRM's access control and persists in inboxes, mobile previews, forwards, and backups. In a diplomatically sensitive setting, a message saying relationship with Country X is cold is itself sensitive. If the coordinator has lost access, or the mail goes to a personal or shared mailbox, it leaks. The proposal states in-app notification and email are both sent, and offers email as a given if it exists. There is no minimal-content email, such as a generic 'you have a new alert, sign in to view'. Reuse of an existing channel does not guarantee it is safe for this content.
challenges.evaluation_of_proposer: The proposer assumes that reusing existing delivery channels bounds exposure. Email content is not governed by Country permissions once sent.

challenge_responses.response: The day-one storm is real and the fix is cheap. The first nightly run is now a silent baseline: it writes flags and badges but sends no notifications, and only later not-cold to cold transitions alert. Countries with no Engagement on record are shown as 'No engagement logged' and never flagged, so missing data cannot generate alerts. This is a rule in the job, with no new table or screen. I defend the single 90-day threshold: per-country thresholds mean a settings screen someone has to maintain. The baseline badge shows stale countries on day one, and the 10% false-alarm criterion plus feedback link tells us whether to move to tiers in a later release. Whether 90 days is the right number is a business judgement, but it is one config value.

A one-shot alert to a missing or deactivated owner would be silent, so I add a system-filled cold_alerted_at on Country. It is set only when the notification goes to an active coordinator, and the nightly job retries until then. This also enforces exactly-once per episode. The badge and filter stay visible regardless. I do not add fallback recipients, escalation chains or leave handling because they need routing data and per-country maintenance. Residual risk is a coordinator on leave who is still an active user. That is bounded by the badge and filter, and we would add a fallback if the first 60 days show missed alerts. Who the fallback recipient should be is an organisational decision for humans, not a product one.

A derived aggregate that includes Engagements the viewer cannot see leaks their existence, so the nightly job now counts only Engagements visible to everyone who can view the Country under the existing access model. Restricted Engagements never move last_engagement_date or is_cold. That is a filter over existing data, with no per-viewer computation or new RBAC. Residual risk: a country engaged only through restricted Engagements can show cold, which is a bounded false alarm the coordinator can resolve, and is safer than a leak. Which Engagements count as restricted is a security classification decision for humans, not something I define. If Engagement has no record-level restriction in the current model, this change is a no-op.

Zombie Missions and placeholder events are a real false-negative path. The fix is cheap: suppression now applies only while the last logged Engagement is 180 days old or less, and only for Missions that are active or Engagements scheduled within 60 days. Past 180 days the Country is flagged cold regardless. The flag is a rule over existing Mission and Engagement dates, with no per-mission review. A stale Mission can therefore hide a cold country for at most about 90 extra days. cold_since is computed from the day the threshold was crossed, so the flip carries engagement-age context.

A1 deliberately defines cold as absence of recorded contact. Filtering by Engagement type or contact status needs an agreed type taxonomy, a reliable in-post flag on every Contact, and ongoing upkeep, which is expensive and depends on data quality we cannot assume. Contact-level departure alerts and quality weighting are explicitly out of scope. Residual risk is a false negative, where a stale or administrative entry keeps a country warm. It is bounded because the badge shows the last engagement date, so coordinators can see how old and what kind of contact it was. It is also bounded by the 90-day clock, which resets only on a logged Engagement. Evidence to add a filter later: false-negative reports in the feedback channel, or an audit showing a material share of clock-resetting Engagements are bulk or with departed contacts. What counts as a legitimate engagement is a data-governance call for humans.

A generic email is cheap and removes the leak. The email now says only that a new CRM alert is waiting and to sign in, with no country name or cold status. Details appear in the in-app notification and Country record, which are covered by Country permissions. This is a template change on an existing channel. Whether email may carry any CRM alert, even a generic one, is a security policy decision for humans. If it is not allowed, A5 already falls back to in-app and badge only.

challenges.challenge_text: Day-one alert storm from stale or inconsistently logged engagement history across ~100 countries, leading to ignored alerts.
challenges.evaluation_of_proposer: The silent baseline run removes the transition storm. Countries with no engagement on record are never flagged. Countries already cold at launch show a badge but do not generate alerts. The single 90-day threshold is one config value, and the false-alarm feedback criterion gives a tuning signal. This is acceptable for an MVP.

challenges.challenge_text: A one-shot alert to a blank or deactivated coordinator leaves the country cold in silence.
challenges.evaluation_of_proposer: cold_alerted_at stays empty until an active coordinator receives the alert, and the job retries nightly. That closes the silent-loss path and enforces exactly-once delivery. A coordinator on leave who is still an active user is a residual risk, bounded by the badge and filter, and fallback recipients are an organisational decision. Acceptable for an MVP.

challenges.challenge_text: The Engagement filter is good, but S3 suppression still reads Mission and scheduled Engagement data with no visibility filter. Scenario: a user can view Country X but not a restricted Mission. The restricted Mission suppresses the cold flag, or a restricted scheduled Engagement does. X shows 'not cold' despite a visibly old last_engagement_date, so the user infers that a confidential Mission exists. The same inference works in reverse when the Mission closes and the country flips to cold. The same leak applies to the in-app notification and the 'last engaged' date.
challenges.evaluation_of_proposer: The Engagement visibility filter in S2 is the right fix for last_engagement_date. But S2 and S3 apply it only to Engagements. S3 says it 'reads existing Mission/Project data' with no equivalent restriction, so the derived is_cold value can still leak restricted Mission activity. The fix is solvable: count only Missions and scheduled Engagements visible to everyone who can view the Country, and add this to the permission-test success criterion.

The rule reads existing Mission/Project data only, and counts only Missions and scheduled Engagements that are visible to every user who can view the Country under the existing access model, so restricted Missions or scheduled Engagements never suppress or release the flag.

When a Country transitions from not-cold to cold, send one in-app notification and one email to the Regional Coordinator assigned to that Country. Fires once per transition, with no repeat reminders. The first nightly run after launch is a silent baseline: it writes flags and badges but sends no notifications, and alerts fire only for transitions seen after it. If the Country has no assigned coordinator or the coordinator's user is deactivated, the alert is not marked as sent (cold_alerted_at stays empty) and delivery is retried each night until an active coordinator exists. The in-app notification shows the country name, last engagement date and a record link. The email is generic and contains no country name or cold status ('You have a new CRM alert, sign in to view').

Show a read-only 'Cold' badge and 'last engaged N days ago' on the existing Country record and in the existing Country list view, and make it filterable. The badge and alert content use the existing Country access permissions, so users who cannot view a Country cannot see its cold status or alerts.
The flag clears automatically the next nightly run after any new Engagement is logged for the Country. No acknowledge, snooze or dismiss workflow.

assumptions.statement: 'Cold' means time elapsed since the last logged Engagement with the country, i.e. an absence of recorded contact, and not a qualitative judgement of relationship quality or sentiment.
assumptions.rationale: Elapsed time is computable from data the CRM already holds, so it needs no new entities and no coordinator input, and is explainable to any user in one sentence.

assumptions.statement: A single global 90-day threshold is an acceptable starting default for all ~100 countries, and the existing Engagement history is logged consistently enough for it to be meaningful.
assumptions.rationale: A single constant avoids a per-country settings screen that someone would have to maintain. The threshold is a single config value that can be tuned after observing real alert volumes, so it is cheap to correct after launch.

assumptions.statement: Every Country already has a Regional Coordinator (or equivalent owner) in the CRM, and the existing Country/Mission access model governs who may view a Country and its data.
assumptions.rationale: Reusing existing ownership and permissions means no routing tables or new RBAC. Alerts go to people who already have rights to the data, which bounds exposure.

assumptions.statement: Active Missions and scheduled future Engagements indicate a live relationship, so a country with them should not be flagged cold even if no Engagement was recently logged.
assumptions.rationale: This is a simple query over existing Mission/Project data that prevents the most obvious false alarms and alert fatigue, without any manual exemption flag.

assumptions.statement: The CRM already has in-app notification and email delivery capability that can be reused. If not, in-app notification and the badge alone are sufficient for v1.
assumptions.rationale: Reusing existing delivery channels avoids building new infrastructure. The badge and filter on the Country list work even without email.

success_criteria.criterion: The nightly job evaluates 100% of active Countries and completes within 15 minutes, with is_cold and last_engagement_date matching a manual spot-check of 20 sampled countries with zero discrepancies.

The first post-launch nightly run sends zero notifications. After that, each not-cold to cold transition produces exactly one notification to an active assigned Regional Coordinator within 24 hours, with zero repeat alerts for the same cold episode, verified in the first 30 days post-launch.

For Countries with a blank or deactivated coordinator in test, no alert is marked sent, and the alert is delivered on the first nightly run after an active coordinator is assigned, in 100% of test cases.

Fewer than 10% of cold alerts in the first 60 days are reported by Regional Coordinators as false alarms (e.g., relationship was active but engagement was not logged), measured via a one-click 'not useful' link or a short feedback survey, used to decide whether to tune the threshold.
A user without access to a given Country sees no cold badge, filter result, or notification for it, verified with a permission test covering at least 3 role types.

In a permission test, adding or removing an Engagement restricted under the existing access model changes no derived Country field (last_engagement_date, is_cold) visible to a user who lacks access to that Engagement, in 100% of test cases.

In a permission test, opening, closing, or scheduling a Mission or future Engagement that is restricted under the existing access model changes no derived Country field (is_cold, cold_since) and triggers no notification visible to a user who lacks access to it, in 100% of test cases.

A Country with an open Mission or a scheduled future Engagement and a last logged Engagement older than 180 days is flagged cold in 100% of test cases, and one with a last Engagement of 100 days or less is suppressed.
Every alert email sent in testing contains no country name and no cold status, only the generic sign-in prompt, in 100% of sampled emails.
After a new Engagement is logged for a cold Country, the cold flag clears by the next nightly run in 100% of test cases, with zero coordinator actions required.

challenge_responses.response: The Critic is right: S2 filtered Engagements but S3 still read Missions and scheduled Engagements unfiltered, so a restricted Mission could suppress or release the flag and reveal its existence. The fix is cheap and uses the same rule as S2. S3 now counts only Missions and scheduled Engagements visible to everyone who can view the Country under the existing access model. It is one more visibility predicate in the existing nightly query, with no new table, per-viewer computation or RBAC. I added a permission-test success criterion for restricted Missions and scheduled Engagements, linked to S3 and S5. The in-app notification and last-engaged date derive only from the filtered values, so they are covered. Residual risk: a Country whose only live activity is restricted can show cold, which is a bounded false alarm the coordinator can resolve, and is safer than a leak. Which Missions or Engagements count as restricted is a security classification decision for humans. If the current model has no record-level restriction on these entities, this change is a no-op.

challenges.challenge_text: Launch-time transition storm from stale or inconsistently logged engagement history across ~100 countries.
challenges.evaluation_of_proposer: Previously accepted. The silent baseline run in S4 removes the day-one storm, and the 10% false-alarm criterion plus the tunable threshold bound the rest. Remains accepted.

challenges.challenge_text: A one-time alert goes to a departed, deactivated or blank coordinator, so the country stays cold with nobody told.
challenges.evaluation_of_proposer: S4 now leaves cold_alerted_at empty and retries nightly until an active coordinator exists, so the alert is no longer lost. A matching test criterion covers blank and deactivated coordinators. A stale but still-active coordinator and fallback recipients are explicitly out of scope, which is acceptable for an MVP. The risk is now bounded.

challenges.challenge_text: Derived last_engagement_date, is_cold and cold_since on the Country could reveal restricted Engagements, Missions or scheduled Engagements to users who can view the Country but not those records.
challenges.evaluation_of_proposer: S2 and S3 now count only Engagements, Missions and scheduled Engagements visible to every user who can view the Country. This is a single computed value, with no per-viewer recomputation and no new RBAC. Permission tests cover both Engagements and Missions. The residual false-cold case is a bounded false alarm, and it is safer than a leak. Which records count as restricted is a classification decision for humans and is rightly out of scope. Acceptable for an MVP.

challenges.challenge_text: Zombie Missions or placeholder future Engagements suppress the cold flag indefinitely, hiding a country with no real contact.
challenges.evaluation_of_proposer: S3 adds a hard cap. Once the last logged Engagement is older than 180 days, the country is flagged cold regardless of open Missions or scheduled Engagements. A test criterion verifies this at the 100-day and 180-day boundaries. This bounds suppression and prevents an abrupt unexplained flip, so the risk is adequately bounded.

challenges.challenge_text: Engagements with departed contacts or administrative entries reset the clock and make a country look warm.
challenges.evaluation_of_proposer: Previously accepted. The defense stands for an MVP, and the feedback loop on false alarms covers the remaining risk. Remains accepted.

challenges.challenge_text: Email carrying the country name and cold status leaks sensitive relationship information outside CRM access controls.
challenges.evaluation_of_proposer: S4 now sends a generic email with no country name or cold status, and the details stay in-app behind access control. A test criterion checks the email content. Whether email may carry any CRM alert is correctly left to institutional policy and is out of scope. The risk is acceptable.

C1.challenge_text: The first nightly run after launch will flag every country whose engagement history is stale or was never logged consistently. Backfill is explicitly out of scope, and some countries are legitimately contacted only once or twice a year. Regional Coordinators across ~100 countries could receive dozens of 'cold' alerts on day one, most of them data-quality artifacts rather than real cooling. They learn to ignore the alert, and the real cold country is missed. A single 90-day threshold also fires constantly for low-tempo relationships and never for high-tempo ones. The 10% false-alarm criterion is measured only after 60 days of damage. There is no launch-time baselining or suppression of the initial transition storm.

C2.challenge_text: The alert goes once, to the single assigned Regional Coordinator, with no repeats. Coordinators turn over often across 100 countries. If the coordinator has left, is on leave, or the assignment is blank or stale, the one-time alert goes to a deactivated mailbox or nobody. Because the alert fires only once per transition, the country then stays cold in silence and nobody is ever told. The assumption that every Country has a valid, current owner is untested, and the design has no fallback recipient or 'no owner' detection.

C3.challenge_text: The derived last_engagement_date and is_cold are computed by a nightly job over ALL Engagement records for a country, then shown to anyone who can view the Country. Under least-privilege, a staff member may see a Country but not a restricted Mission, Contact, or Engagement. A user who sees 'last engaged 2 days ago' on a country where they know of no recent activity learns that a confidential engagement occurred. The same applies to a country that silently flips from cold to warm. S5 says Country permissions apply, but it does not say the derived value is computed per viewer's visible engagements or that restricted engagements are excluded or masked. The system-filled field on the Country entity bypasses record-level restrictions.

C4.challenge_text: Suppression of the cold flag while a country has any 'active Mission' or any scheduled future Engagement creates false negatives. Missions are often left open long after real activity stops, and future engagements are often placeholders that get cancelled or never marked complete. A country with a zombie mission or a stale calendar entry is never flagged, even after a year of no real contact. This is exactly the relationship the feature should catch. When the mission is eventually closed, the country may flip to cold abruptly, with no engagement-age context. The proposal has no staleness bound on the suppressing mission or scheduled engagement, such as a cap on how long it can suppress.

C5.challenge_text: The rule counts 'any Contact, any channel' as warming the relationship. An engagement logged with a ministry contact who has since left office, with a mission delegate unrelated to the host government, or a bulk or administrative entry such as a mass circular or an internal note logged as an Engagement, resets the 90-day clock. The country shows 'not cold' even though there is no live channel to anyone currently in post. Conversely, a country engaged only through a single departed minister's staff looks warm. 'Absence of recorded contact' is not the same as a working relationship when contact turnover is the main real-world risk. There is no filter on engagement type or on whether the contact is still active.

C6.challenge_text: S4 sends email containing the country name and 'gone cold' status. Email leaves the CRM's access control and persists in inboxes, mobile previews, forwards, and backups. In a diplomatically sensitive setting, a message saying relationship with Country X is cold is itself sensitive. If the coordinator has lost access, or the mail goes to a personal or shared mailbox, it leaks. The proposal states in-app notification and email are both sent, and offers email as a given if it exists. There is no minimal-content email, such as a generic 'you have a new alert, sign in to view'. Reuse of an existing channel does not guarantee it is safe for this content.

final_decision.feature_request: The CRM should alert us when our relationship with a country goes cold.
final_decision.executive_summary: v1 will flag a Country as cold when its most recent logged Engagement is older than a single global 90-day threshold. A nightly job writes system-filled fields on the existing Country entity, shows a read-only Cold badge and filter, and sends one in-app notification and one generic email to the assigned Regional Coordinator per transition, with the first post-launch run acting as a silent baseline. Suppression for active Missions or scheduled Engagements is capped at 180 days, and only records visible to every user who can view the Country are counted. The main trade-off argued was alert accuracy and relationship coverage versus simplicity and confidentiality: restricted records and sensitive email content were handled by narrowing what the job counts and what the email says, rather than by adding configuration or workflow. All six challenges ended ACCEPTED, no scope or success criteria are pending, and no issues were escalated, so no human decision is outstanding.
agreed_scope_included: [S1] Define 'cold' as a deterministic rule over existing Engagement records: a country is cold when its most recent logged Engagement (any Contact, any Project or Mission, any channel) is older than a single global threshold of 90 days. No new fields for Regional Coordinators to fill in.

[S2] A nightly scheduled job evaluates every active Country against the S1 rule and writes derived, system-filled fields (last_engagement_date, is_cold, cold_since, cold_alerted_at) on the existing Country entity. No new tables and no manual input. The job counts only Engagements that are visible to every user who can view the Country under the existing access model, so Engagements restricted under that model never influence the derived values. A Country with no Engagement on record shows 'No engagement logged' and is never flagged cold or alerted.

[S3] Suppress the cold flag while a Country has an active Mission, or a Mission/Project Engagement scheduled within the next 60 days, since the relationship is evidently being worked. Suppression has a hard cap: once the last logged Engagement is older than 180 days (2x threshold), the Country is flagged cold regardless of open Missions or scheduled Engagements. The rule reads existing Mission/Project data only, and counts only Missions and scheduled Engagements that are visible to every user who can view the Country under the existing access model, so restricted Missions or scheduled Engagements never suppress or release the flag.

[S4] When a Country transitions from not-cold to cold, send one in-app notification and one email to the Regional Coordinator assigned to that Country. Fires once per transition, with no repeat reminders. The first nightly run after launch is a silent baseline: it writes flags and badges but sends no notifications, and alerts fire only for transitions seen after it. If the Country has no assigned coordinator or the coordinator's user is deactivated, the alert is not marked as sent (cold_alerted_at stays empty) and delivery is retried each night until an active coordinator exists. The in-app notification shows the country name, last engagement date and a record link. The email is generic and contains no country name or cold status ('You have a new CRM alert, sign in to view').

[S5] Show a read-only 'Cold' badge and 'last engaged N days ago' on the existing Country record and in the existing Country list view, and make it filterable. The badge and alert content use the existing Country access permissions, so users who cannot view a Country cannot see its cold status or alerts.
[S6] The flag clears automatically the next nightly run after any new Engagement is logged for the Country. No acknowledge, snooze or dismiss workflow.
